https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-.text: German defense entrepreneur Stefan Thumann argued sabotage operations carried out by Moscow against his country are an “act of war … controlled and coordinated here by the Russian armed forces.” Speaking exclusively with Paul Ronzheimer of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network in a podcast episode released Tuesday, Thumann rejected the “hybrid war” label used by EU leaders to describe the Kremlin’s campaign in Europe. “Germany and Russia are at war,” he insisted. Advertisement Advertisement The warning lands as Berlin hardens its stance on suspected Russian sabotage. Chancellor Friedrich Merz is preparing to blame Moscow for an attempted drone attack in Leipzig and unveil “extensive” sanctions, officials told POLITICO and WELT AM SONNTAG. Thumann’s company, Donaustahl, supplies combat drones to Ukraine, according to the executive. He says he has been forced to live under round-the-clock protection after authorities uncovered an alleged Russian intelligence plan to poison him in 2025. Authorities warned him shortly before Christmas that he could be in danger. “Yes, it comes from Russia. And yes, it is very serious — your life is at risk,” he said they told him. Within days, a suspected low-level operative had been detained. Thumann said he had turned official addresses into surveillance-heavy “honeypots” — locations deliberately designed to lure hostile actors into a trap. “The low-level operatives were only there to find out where I was,” he added. “Then an assassination using poison was supposed to be carried out.” The threat has upended his life. Thumann said he now lives at undisclosed locations with bodyguards, has not seen his family for months, and has prepared a will and advance health care directive in case he is killed. https://www.politico.eu/article/the-poli.text: LIVERPOOL, England — Seven out of ten voters want the government to build a closer relationship with the European Union, according to a new POLITICO Poll that shows the extent of support for overhauling the Brexit settlement. Even among voters who support Brexit campaigner Nigel Farage’s Reform UK party, a majority — 51% — share the view that the current arrangement with Brussels is too distant. The poll comes at a highly sensitive moment for the U.K.’s governing Labour Party, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham facing demands from some senior colleagues to reverse Brexit and rejoin the EU. Advertisement Advertisement “The public now often looks to Europe for overseas alliances, particularly as the U.S. is increasingly perceived as at best unreliable and at worst adversarial,” said Seb Wride, head of polling at public research company Public First, which conducted the poll for POLITICO. “But it’s not straightforward for the government. ‘Getting closer with Europe’ is not the same as ‘reversing Brexit,’ and Burnham will have a challenging needle to thread to appease his pro-European wings without reopening wounds the public would prefer stayed closed.” The Brexit referendum a decade ago divided the country, cost two prime ministers their jobs and triggered often bad-tempered divorce negotiations between London and Brussels that took years to complete. Public First asked respondents for their views on moving the country closer to the EU and accepting EU rules. Some 31% said Britain should build a “closer” relationship with Brussels, but only if it did not mean complying with the EU’s rulebook. But 39% wanted “much closer” cooperation even if that did require the U.K. to follow some EU rules again. The poll also confirms how the Brexit debate has carved the country into two blocs — pro and anti. Supporters of parties on the left were far more likely to back a closer EU relationship than those on the right. Green Party voters were the keenest of all: 64% said they’d support much closer EU ties even if that meant applying more EU rules. Older voters were less keen on closer ties to Brussels. Among Reform UK voters, 51% said they want a closer relationship — twice the 25% who want more distance from the EU. That poses a potential challenge for party leader Farage, a career Euroskeptic. The finding could also provide ammunition for Labour politicians who want Burnham to be more ambitious about his plans to upgrade the U.K.-EU relationship, potentially including a return to the bloc’s customs union, single market or even full EU membership again. As Burnham prepared to deliver his Tuesday speech to party members and activists in Liverpool, a succession of ministers and others gave their views about what kind of closer relationship with the EU he should pursue. Advertisement Advertisement Former Prime Minister Tony Blair published a report urging Burnham to put rejoining a reformed EU on the agenda for the next decade. In an interview at the POLITICO Pub in Liverpool on Monday, Mayor of London Sadiq Khan called on the prime minister to begin the debate about rejoining the EU immediately, saying Brexit has been “a disaster” and “the biggest act of economic self-harm any country has ever done.” “At some stage, sooner or later, we’ll be having the conversation about rejoining the European Union,” Khan said. “Why wait?” Public First surveyed 2,028 U.K. adults online Sept. 13-15, 2026.
